title: Nand Lal's kitchen
hookLine: tradition says the Guru praised Nand Lal's langar above others because it served everyone, anytime

lines: THE CHAIRS ARE UP ON THE TABLES.
cards: The dinner rush is over. Chairs are up on the tables, the floor is wet, the cook is wiping down the last pan. A traveler knocks on the glass.
Kitchen's closed, someone mouths, pointing at the sign with the hours. Nobody is being cruel. Hours are hours.
Sikh tradition keeps a story about a kitchen with no such sign. It belonged to the Persian poet we met a few days ago, the one who served at Guru Gobind Singh's court. Today: langar.

teach.h: THE GURU GOES ROUND IN DISGUISE.
teach.b: This story comes to us as a sakhi, a story passed on, not from Nand Lal's own poems. At Anandpur, tradition says, several Sikhs ran langars, free kitchens.
The Guru wanted to see what they were really like, so he went round them dressed as an ordinary traveler, at an hour when no meal was being served.
At one door he was told to come back later. At another, the food wasn't ready, so there was nothing to give.
Then he came to Nand Lal's kitchen, and whatever was in the pots, finished or not, was put in front of him straight away. Later, the story goes, the Guru praised Nand Lal's langar above the others.
Not because the food was finer. Because it served everyone, anytime. A few things are folded into that.
Hunger doesn't keep office hours: someone who arrives late is exactly as hungry as someone who arrives on time. The other kitchens weren't wicked; they were organized.
The story isn't against good planning, only against the plan becoming a reason to send someone away. Nand Lal didn't wait for the meal to be perfect.

teach.h: NAND LAL SERVES WHAT THERE IS.
teach.b: He gave what there was, as it was.
And notice who the traveler turned out to be.

In Sikh telling, the one you serve at the odd hour may be the Guru himself, so the langar never needs to check. A gurdwara langar keeps the same idea today: food for whoever walks in, without asking who they are.

how: Gurdwara langars serve free food to anyone who comes, and Sikhs retell the story of Bhai Nand Lal's kitchen as a picture of a langar that never turns anyone away.

o: a free kitchen that feeds anyone who comes
a set meal served only at festival times
a kitchen run by the Guru's own family

games.q: inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: served what there was, straight away

s: in the story, the Guru praised Nand Lal's food for being the finest
he praised the kitchen because it served everyone, anytime, with whatever was there.
the story comes down as a sakhi rather than from Nand Lal's own poems
it's told and retold in Sikh tradition about the poet's langar.
the story is against planning meals
the other kitchens were organized; the point is not letting the plan send someone away.

games.q: you run a free kitchen. the meal is over, the pots are half-cooked for tomorrow, and a traveler asks for food. what do you do?
o: ask them to come back at mealtime.
serve what's in the pots, as it is.
games.why: in the story, Nand Lal's kitchen served what there was straight away, and the traveler turned out to be the Guru.

practice: Picture who might turn up hungry outside the usual hours, a roommate coming in late, a coworker who skipped lunch, a delivery driver, and choose one.
Then choose what you already have, fruit, tea, leftovers, as they are, and picture handing it over without asking anything first. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you picture it.

wordCard.voice: Langar, the free kitchen that, in the story, fed a stranger at the wrong hour with whatever was in the pots, and was praised for it.

carryVoice: Your line: serve anytime. Hunger keeps no office hours, and neither did his kitchen. See you tomorrow.
